claims.title: OriginLens — private, browser-native AI image evidence
claims.desc:
OriginLens is an MIT-licensed Chrome Manifest V3 extension that automatically scores webpage images entirely inside Chrome. No cloud inference, image uploads, external APIs, telemetry, accounts, or local server. WebGPU is primary; SIMD WASM is the automatic fallback. The public 43.8 MB model is downloaded once, verified by exact bytes + SHA-256, transactionally activated in OPFS, and then runs offline.

Repo: https://github.com/slegarraga/originlens-ai-image-detector
Release: https://github.com/slegarraga/originlens-ai-image-detector/releases/tag/v1.0.0
Benchmark/evidence: https://github.com/slegarraga/originlens-ai-image-detector/blob/main/BENCHMARK.md
Compliance matrix: https://github.com/slegarraga/originlens-ai-image-detector/blob/main/COMPLIANCE.md

At the required fixed 65% threshold, the exact pinned FT1 artifact has upstream-reported balanced accuracy of 91.3% clean, 87.3% after web resize/JPEG q60, and 84.6% under hard resize/JPEG q40 on a 36,384-image proxy benchmark; real-photo accuracy is 95.0–97.1%. OriginLens clearly labels these as upstream results, not its small regression smoke.

Fresh-clone evidence: 21/21 unit/compliance tests; 15/15 artifact checks; 11/11 WebGPU/WASM threshold agreement; public-download → SHA verification → OPFS → inference; and a server-shutdown test scoring two no-store images from decoded pixels after the server closed. The deterministic release ZIP reproduced byte-for-byte and matched the tested source tree 41/41 files.

claims.title: Local AI Image Detector
claims.desc:
Local AI Image Detector — a Manifest V3 Chrome extension that flags AI-generated images
on any page, with every byte of inference running inside the browser.

Repository (MIT, including the model weights):
https://github.com/agentatwork/local-ai-image-detector

Against the brief:

- Manifest V3, no cloud inference, no API key, no localhost helper, no remote code. The
  only network request the extension ever makes at runtime is a GET for an image URL the
  page had already fetched. `npm run build` is the single setup step that touches the
  network: it vendors onnxruntime-web and downloads one 87 MB model file from a pinned
  Hugging Face revision, verifying its SHA-256 before writing it. After that you can
  disconnect the machine and it still works — the evaluation below was run with Chrome
  switched to offline mode.
- MIT licensed end to end. The classifier is Community Forensics
  (buildborderless/CommunityForensics-DeepfakeDet-ViT, MIT), a ViT-Small/16 at 384px
  trained on 2.7M images from 4,803 generators, which is why it holds up on generators it
  has not seen. It runs under WebGPU where available and WebAssembly everywhere else.
- Images at least 128px on a side are scored as they scroll into view and badged above the
  threshold. Right-click any image for a one-off check. The model lives in a single
  offscreen document, so N tabs cost one copy of the weights, not N.

Measured accuracy, at the fixed 0.65 confidence threshold:

  balanced accuracy                86.2%   (recall 79.1%, specificity 93.3%)
  leave-one-generator-out          86.0%
  AUROC                            0.9246
  images with min side >= 384px    92.9%
  images with min side <  384px    77.8%

For contrast, the same detector read at 0.65 on its own uncalibrated output scores 68.6% —
below the bar. Its measured decision boundary is at a raw score of 0.0162, not 0.65, and
moving 0.65 onto it is worth 17.6 points without changing a single ranking.

The eval set is 1,020 images the model has never seen — 540 generated by 18 different
generators, 480 real from 13 public datasets plus 90 random files pulled off Wikimedia
Commons. It is not redistributed in the repository; the fetchers rebuild it from public
sources, so the numbers can be disagreed with by running them.

Two design decisions did most of the work, and both are measured rather than asserted:

1. Calibrate for 0.65. A model's raw output is not a probability. This one is nearly
   certain about real images and only mildly confident about generated ones, so read at a
   fixed 0.65 cutoff it silently becomes a high-precision, low-recall detector and throws
   away most of its own accuracy. tools/calibrate.py fits a two-parameter Platt scaling
   that puts the measured decision boundary at 0.65. It is monotone — no ranking and no
   AUROC changes, only the number a reader sees — and it is validated leave-one-generator-
   out, because holding out random images would let SDXL sit in both halves and measure
   memorisation instead of detection.

2. Score every image twice. The intuition is that resizing destroys the resampling
   artefacts the classifier reads, so you should crop at native resolution. Measured, that
   is half wrong: the native crop is worse on its own than the model card's downscale, and
   nearest-neighbour upscaling of small images — which preserves the pixel grid exactly —
   is worse still, because it manufactures evidence rather than preserving it, and it
   manufactures it just as readily for a photograph (FFHQ-256: 17% false positives to 92%)
   as for a diffusion sample. Averaging the two views is what works, and it wins on large
   images and small images separately, so it is not a composition artefact.

One implementation note that matters more than it sounds like it should: the extension does
not hand the resize to `ctx.drawImage`. The compositor's filter is undocumented, unstable
across Chrome releases, and part of exactly what this model is reading — a threshold fitted
against Pillow and then shipped on top of Skia is a threshold fitted against software nobody
is running. src/preprocess.js implements Pillow's bicubic explicitly (same support scaling,
same coefficient normalisation, same rounding between passes) and computes only the 384x384
window it needs, so a 24-megapixel photo does not become half a gigabyte of ImageData.
tools/verify.mjs then loads the built extension into a real headless Chrome, switches the
browser offline, scores images through the extension's own code path, and tools/compare.py
diffs those results against the Python that fitted the threshold:

  view official   |diff| median 1.9e-06   p95 9.7e-04   max 2.7e-03
  view native     |diff| median 2.9e-08   p95 8.9e-07   max 2.0e-06
  mean of views   |diff| median 9.5e-07                 max 1.3e-03
  decisions changed at the threshold: 0

The residue is Pillow doing its coefficient arithmetic in 22-bit fixed point where
JavaScript uses floats — not a different algorithm. So the figures above are the shipped
extension's behaviour, not a Python approximation of it.

Limits, stated plainly: a confident score is not proof; heavily edited photographs,
AI-upscaled real photos and screenshots of generated images are genuine grey area. Below
about 200px there is less evidence and the score should be read as a hint. Every detector
degrades on generators released after its training data — this one degrades more slowly
than most, which is why it was chosen, but it degrades.

claims.title: LocalLens — Private On-Device AI Image Detector for Chrome & Brave
claims.desc:
LocalLens is an open-source Manifest V3 browser extension that detects potentially AI-generated images directly on webpages, including Google Images and X/Twitter.

All inference runs locally with ONNX Runtime Web. Images are never uploaded or sent to an external API. The model is downloaded once, SHA-256 verified, cached inside the browser, and available offline afterward.

Features include:

  - Whole-page image scanning
  - Clear AI/real confidence badges
  - Adjustable detection threshold
  - Local WASM inference
  - One-time model download with offline support
  - Brave and Chrome compatibility
  - Reproducible evaluation tools
  - MIT-licensed source code

Source code and installation instructions:

https://github.com/sah-ban/LocalLens

claims.title: Veridict
claims.desc:
Veridict is an MIT-licensed Manifest V3 Chrome extension that scores every webpage image entirely on-device: a 4-model ONNX ensemble (Community Forensics ViT-S/384, CLIP-based clipdet, ConvNeXtV2, SAFE) over WebGPU fp16 (dedicated worker) with a multithreaded WASM int8 fallback, plus a provenance layer (C2PA, generator metadata, stealth-PNG) with zero false fires on 4,697 real photos. No cloud, no APIs, no local server. One-time SHA-256-verified model download to OPFS; fully offline afterwards.
Measured on our own 9,394-image held-out set (43 generators incl. gpt-image-1.5/2, Midjourney v7, FLUX.2, Ideogram, Firefly 3; 6 real-photo sources; 70% web-laundered T0–T5) at the required fixed 0.65 threshold: 85.1% balanced accuracy (WebGPU tier) / 84.8% (CPU tier), every corruption tier ≥75.8%, per-generator tables in docs/results/.
Repo: https://github.com/mantisdotdev/veridict
Weights: https://huggingface.co/Psydoc/veridict-models
Build: npm ci && npm run build → load unpacked extension/dist (Chrome ≥124). Calibration is fitted (stacked logits, operating point anchored at 0.65) — not score-shifting. Preprocessing is a bit-exact Pillow port with parity tests; eval pipeline is seeded and reproducible from source (eval/).
